@Veltrona8  This is a very romantic take on “deep tech,” but it confuses ideology with execution.

No country builds semiconductor ecosystems through vibes, speeches, or activist energy. They do it through coordination: government + industry + global partners + capital + regulation + talent pipelines. That’s not “maintaining the old system”, that is how Taiwan, Korea, Japan, and even the US actually built theirs.

Real deep tech starts with people who understand how large systems work in practice: supply chains, procurement, IP licensing, cross-border partnerships, risk management, and scaling. That’s why seasoned operators matter. Experience isn’t cosmetic, it’s compounding.

Ironically, the belief that “managers can’t transform” is exactly what people say before they’ve ever built anything at scale.

Also, let’s be honest: writing ambitious policy decks about semiconductors ≠ understanding semiconductor manufacturing. The gap between theory and delivery is where most “revolutionary” ideas quietly die.

Transformation doesn’t come from rejecting the system.
It comes from knowing it well enough to bend it.

That’s why I back teams who’ve actually worked across industries, borders, and crises …not those still auditioning in the comment section.

Comment Text:
⁠Fair point, and I appreciate the respectful tone despite our differing political views. As Thais, we both want what’s best for the country. Thailand absolutely cannot afford sugarcoating, especially in critical ministries. But I strongly disagree that Bhumjaithai is just three faces for optics.

What gives me confidence is the depth behind the scenes: seasoned technocrats, private-sector operators, and professionals who have actually built and delivered in the real world. Governance is execution, not stage performance.

This is also why, for this round, I don’t see the People Party as suitable. Their core strength is activism and messaging — not coalition-building, not execution, and not working constructively with industry or institutions. That may work in opposition politics, but it’s a high-risk approach for governing in a volatile global environment.

Real transformation doesn’t come from shouting “revolution” louder. It comes from cooperation with the private sector, global partners, engineers, and operators who’ve built and delivered success before.

Leaders like Khun Supagee matter not just for their resumes, but because they attract other high-caliber people into advisory and execution roles. Talent follows credibility. Ecosystems don’t form around slogans.

Thailand isn’t a campus debate or a policy lab experiment. It doesn’t need a protest movement in power right now. Thailand needs a team that can keep the system running while upgrading it responsibly with competence, stability, and respect for institutions. 

That’s why, this time, I choose execution over theatrics.
